title: Composite
summary: Treat a single item and a group of items through one interface.

parts.rule: Composite gives a leaf and a container the same component interface. A container holds child components and implements an operation by combining the children's results. Because a child may itself be a container, the same client call works at any level of the tree.
parts.why: Hierarchical data often produces two parallel code paths: one for a single item and another for a group. A shared component operation moves that recursion into the data structure. The benefit is uniform traversal; the risk is hiding a large tree walk behind a method that looks cheap.
parts.example: A storage browser defines Entry.sizeBytes() and Entry.render(indent). File is a leaf: report.pdf returns 2,000,000 bytes. Folder is a composite: it stores a list of Entry children and sums sizeBytes() across them. The root folder contains report.pdf plus a photos folder. photos contains a.jpg at 3,000,000 bytes and b.jpg at 5,000,000 bytes, so photos.sizeBytes() returns 8,000,000 and root.sizeBytes() returns 10,000,000. The caller does not branch on file versus folder; it asks any Entry for its size. render(0) works the same way: File renders one line, while Folder renders its name and then calls child.render(1). Adding a nested archive folder requires no new traversal case. Complexity is still O(n) for n entries, and recursion uses O(h) stack space for height h. If the UI calls sizeBytes() 60 times per second on a million-entry tree, that uniform method hides expensive repeated work; cache totals and invalidate them when a child changes, or compute them outside the render loop. A flat shopping cart with 12 products and no nested bundles needs only a list and sum, not a composite hierarchy.
parts.use: Use composite when the domain is genuinely recursive and clients perform the same operation on an item or a group: file trees, scene graphs, menu trees, product bundles, and organization units. Keep the component interface small, and document whether each operation visits the whole subtree.
parts.refuse: Prefer a list plus a loop when the data is flat. Do not force unrelated leaf types into a vague interface merely to reuse traversal code. Watch for cycles if children can be attached freely, and avoid presenting O(n) recursive work as a constant-time getter. Uniform syntax does not make every component operation equally cheap.

body:
Rule. Composite gives a leaf and a container the same component interface. A container holds child components and implements an operation by combining the children's results. Because a child may itself be a container, the same client call works at any level of the tree.

Why it matters. Hierarchical data often produces two parallel code paths: one for a single item and another for a group. A shared component operation moves that recursion into the data structure. The benefit is uniform traversal; the risk is hiding a large tree walk behind a method that looks cheap.

Worked example. A storage browser defines Entry.sizeBytes() and Entry.render(indent). File is a leaf: report.pdf returns 2,000,000 bytes. Folder is a composite: it stores a list of Entry children and sums sizeBytes() across them. The root folder contains report.pdf plus a photos folder. photos contains a.jpg at 3,000,000 bytes and b.jpg at 5,000,000 bytes, so photos.sizeBytes() returns 8,000,000 and root.sizeBytes() returns 10,000,000. The caller does not branch on file versus folder; it asks any Entry for its size. render(0) works the same way: File renders one line, while Folder renders its name and then calls child.render(1). Adding a nested archive folder requires no new traversal case. Complexity is still O(n) for n entries, and recursion uses O(h) stack space for height h. If the UI calls sizeBytes() 60 times per second on a million-entry tree, that uniform method hides expensive repeated work; cache totals and invalidate them when a child changes, or compute them outside the render loop. A flat shopping cart with 12 products and no nested bundles needs only a list and sum, not a composite hierarchy.

[[diagram:tree]]

When to use. Use composite when the domain is genuinely recursive and clients perform the same operation on an item or a group: file trees, scene graphs, menu trees, product bundles, and organization units. Keep the component interface small, and document whether each operation visits the whole subtree.

When to refuse. Prefer a list plus a loop when the data is flat. Do not force unrelated leaf types into a vague interface merely to reuse traversal code. Watch for cycles if children can be attached freely, and avoid presenting O(n) recursive work as a constant-time getter. Uniform syntax does not make every component operation equally cheap.
